entities.summary:
Eadberht III Præn was the King of Kent from 796 to 798, marking the last time Kent existed as an independent kingdom. He was the leader of a rebellion against Mercia's hegemony, which had dominated Kent since the 7th century. The rebellion was sparked by a combination of economic and political factors, including Mercia's increasing demands for tribute and Kent's growing resentment towards Mercian rule.

This brief reign had significant consequences, including the eventual downfall of Kent's independence and its absorption into the Kingdom of Wessex. Eadberht III Præn's actions also had a lasting impact on the region's politics and culture, contributing to the rise of the Wessex monarchy and shaping the course of Kentish identity.

In the words of the 10th-century historian, 'The works of Eadberht III Præn are a testament to the enduring power of Kentish resistance against Mercian dominance.'

The rebellion, led by Eadberht III Prån, was sparked by Mercia's encroachment on Kent's territories. Eadberht III Prån's brief reign was ultimately unsuccessful, as Mercia regained control of Kent shortly after his death. 

Despite the short duration of his reign, Eadberht III Prån's legacy continues to be felt in the region. The rebellion he led contributed to the fragmentation of Anglo-Saxon England, setting the stage for the Norman Conquest in 1066. 

In conclusion, Eadberht III Prån's brief reign as King of Kent was a pivotal moment in the kingdom's history, marking the last time it existed as an independent entity. His rebellion against Mercia's hegemony had significant consequences for the region, shaping the course of English history for centuries to come.
